The biggest shift I've noticed in the Data & AI hiring market over the last month?
 
Permanent Data & AI engineers are now actively seeking contract-only roles. People who've never contracted before are saying they won't consider anything except a day-rate contract.
 
That's new. It used to be permanent candidates who were merely curious about contracting, or "open to both."
 
Here's the theory:
 
For genuinely AI-native engineers with strong data platform fundamentals, the market has shifted hard. They know they're in demand — juggling 5, 10, sometimes 15+ live opportunities at once. Inboxes full.
 
And they see almost zero risk in leaving permanent work for contracting, because they know another opportunity will be waiting before the current one even wraps up.
 
Add eye-watering day rates into that mix, and the real question isn't "why would they contract?" It's "why wouldn't they?"
 
What this means for hiring: attracting AI-native talent is about to get a lot harder.
 
You're not just competing with other local businesses anymore. You're competing with:
 
→ International companies hiring directly out of your market
 → Overseas organizations offering base salaries, equity, and packages local employers can't match
 → Contract opportunities offering serious day rates, flexibility, and real agentic/AI-native builds — not off-the-shelf integrations
 
"Permanent = security" is a much weaker pitch when a sought-after engineer can move into a high day-rate contract and already have the next one lined up a month before this one ends.
 
If your hiring strategy hasn't caught up to this shift yet, it's worth a serious look — the market is moving faster than most playbooks can keep up with.

I have watched prospecting change enormously over the last 15 years. I suspect we will see even greater change over the next two or three.

SCIENCE JUST GOT CHEAPER THAN COFFEE. DID ANYONE NOTICE? $2,000. That's what 10 scientific breakthroughs cost — breakthroughs humanity had struggled with for decades.

On August 1, OpenAI published results from an internal model, Astra: 10 open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science — the Ehrhart volume conjecture, Erdős problems #146, 180, 183, the Closest Vector Problem (the foundation of post-quantum cryptography), the construction of non-sofic groups, and others.

What's fundamentally new isn't the solutions themselves, but how they were published: every proof formalized in Lean 4 and released on GitHub under Apache 2.0, with zero unproven steps. For the first time in AI history, verification requires no trust in the company — only running a compiler. Tim Gowers (Fields Medalist) said he would have recommended the work for publication without hesitation.

Key takeaways for business and professionals:

▪️The cost of research collapsed by orders of magnitude. The "generation → formal verification" pipeline will migrate from math into pharma, logistics, law, and engineering. R&D stops being a privilege of corporations.

▪️Verifiability becomes the standard. When your AI assistant writes code, checks a contract, or computes a financial model — the next generation of models will deliver results not "by feel," but with machine-verifiable correctness proofs.

▪️Competence shifts. Human value lies not in computing, but in framing the right problem and interpreting results. This changes hiring, education, and competitive advantage within a 2–3 year horizon.

Caution is warranted too: the problems were hand-picked, the model is closed, and as Gary Marcus notes, success in formalizable domains doesn't guarantee success in non-formalizable ones. 

But the structural fact remains: machine-verifiable science just became cheaper than its human verification.

“Did you use AI to write your CV??”
 
I supply contractors to organisations across the UK Water Sector, so I speak to clients every day.

We talk about the market, vacancies, Football (now Arsenal are back on top!) and plenty of other things.
 
But one conversation seems to be coming up more and more…

AI x CVs.
 
I genuinely get it. AI is brilliant. I use it a lot myself (mostly for FPL).
  
But there is a problem.
  
If your CV says you’re a “dynamic, results-driven professional with a proven track record of delivering innovative solutions within complex environments”… (I asked AI to write that, by the way.)
  
…I still don't know what you actually did and chances are, I’ve already read something very similar on the last 10 CVs I’ve looked at. As more and more people use AI to create their CV's. 
  
A big part of my job is getting to know people. Understanding what they want, what they’ve actually done, what they’re good at and importantly, what makes them different.
  
I match that up with what my clients needs are now, or what they might need in the future.
 
So for me to do the best job I can for my candidates and clients, I need the detail.
 
Especially when it comes to contract roles in the Water Sector.
 
- Which AMP / framework? 
- What projects have you worked on? 
- Which water companies / contractors? 
-What were you actually responsible for? 
- How big were the projects, and what were they worth? 
- What systems, disciplines or technical experience do you have?
  
That’s the stuff I want to see. Not paragraph's that sounds good but tells me nothing.
  
Use AI to improve your CV. Just don’t let it tell your career story for you. Because AI wasn’t there when you did the work.
